summary:
Libya's Penal Code penalises "illicit sexual intercourse" and "indecent acts", and the indecent-acts provisions carry up to five years' imprisonment. Same-sex relations are not legal for men or women. The sources identify no provision that criminalises homosexuality by that name; enforcement instead runs through the general morality offences. A regional guide published by The Guardian on 21 June 2016 lists Libya among the states where imprisonment is the penalty and notes that where no specific law exists, other laws are used.

Cairo 52's country review records de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process itself, whether social, medical or surgical, enforced through the same indecent-acts and illicit-intercourse provisions. Religious rulings issued in recent years have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible, which narrows the ground on which a trans person can seek or be seen to have undergone care.

Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that same-sex relations are not legal for men or women, that the indecent-acts provisions carry up to five years' imprisonment, and that no legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exist. Same-sex relationships are not legally recognised, and legal gender recognition is unavailable: official identity documents cannot be changed. A visitor whose documents and presentation differ has no domestic procedure to fall back on.

Violence against people perceived as gender-nonconforming has been documented in territory held by armed groups. Human Rights Watch reported on 8 June 2015 that Islamic State killed men accused of homosexuality in areas it controlled, including Derna, where a young man was targeted by local Islamists for effeminate dress and "contemporary" clothes; the case dates from November 2014. D+C reported in June 2015 that Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in Derna in April 2015, and concluded that conditions for homosexuals in Libya were worsening as militias controlled territory.

Earlier vigilante violence is also recorded. On 26 November 2012, HuffPost reported that twelve men accused of being gay faced torture and threats of death at the hands of a Libyan militia, in the early post-revolutionary period.

A 2010 case heard in France concerned a Libyan girl who was jailed, raped and returned to her family for a forced marriage after she stated online that she was gay.
tangentialFactors:
The Guardian's regional guide, published 21 June 2016, places Libya in a group of states where the penalty for homosexuality is imprisonment, and cautions that the specific term varies from country to country and that jurisdictions without a dedicated offence fall back on other laws. The comparison is regional rather than Libya-specific; the guide names no Libyan statute and no term of years.

D+C's June 2015 assessment attributed the deterioration to militia control of territory rather than to a change in statute. The killings recorded in 2014 and 2015 occurred under armed-group territorial control rather than through Libyan courts, a distinct enforcement channel from the penal code.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations cannot register in Libya. There is no registered civil-society infrastructure through which residents can seek support.

Religious rulings that designate gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible bear on residents' access to care, since the same rulings shape what clinicians and families will permit.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2010 asylum account gives no age, schooling or student status for the person concerned, and the sources do not establish whether the case produced a change in Libyan practice.

The sources give a maximum of five years for indecent acts but no maximum term for illicit sexual intercourse, and no Libyan statute criminalising homosexuality by name is identified.

Reporting from Derna in 2015 moved only through the mosque, so the number of killings and assaults recorded for that period is likely incomplete and no reliable count is available.
